lesson.title: Sharing Electrons: Covalent Bonds and the Molecules of Life
lesson.summary: This section explains how covalent bonds form through the sharing of electron pairs, distinguishes nonpolar from polar covalent bonds based on electronegativity, and shows how these bonds build the carbon based molecules central to biology.
lesson.body:
A covalent bond forms when two atoms share a pair of electrons rather than one atom fully transferring an electron to the other, as happens in an ionic bond. Sharing works well when both atoms hold their valence electrons with similar strength, so that neither atom can simply pull the electron away from the other. Because carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen, the elements that dominate biological molecules, generally fall into this category, covalent bonds are the dominant bond type inside the large organic molecules that make up living things, including proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids. A single covalent bond shares one pair of electrons, a double bond shares two pairs, and a triple bond shares three pairs; more shared pairs generally means a shorter, stronger bond between the two atoms involved.

Not all covalent bonds share their electrons equally, and this distinction matters enormously in biology. Electronegativity is a measure of how strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself. When two atoms of similar electronegativity share electrons, such as two carbon atoms bonded together or a carbon atom bonded to a hydrogen atom, the electrons spend roughly equal time near each nucleus, and the bond is called nonpolar covalent. When one atom is considerably more electronegative than the other, such as oxygen bonded to hydrogen or nitrogen bonded to hydrogen, the shared electrons spend more time near the more electronegative atom. This creates a polar covalent bond: the electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge, often written with the Greek letter delta as delta minus, while the other atom carries a partial positive charge, delta plus, even though the molecule as a whole carries no net charge.

A useful example that ties covalent bonding directly to carbon's role, discussed earlier in this chapter under elements of life, is methane, the simplest organic molecule, with the formula CH4. A single carbon atom, with four valence electrons available for bonding, forms four separate nonpolar covalent bonds to four hydrogen atoms, each hydrogen contributing its single electron to complete a shared pair. This arrangement satisfies carbon's need for eight electrons in its outer shell and each hydrogen's need for two, and it illustrates carbon's defining property: the capacity to form four stable covalent bonds, which allows carbon atoms to link to one another in chains, branches, and rings that serve as the backbone for every major class of biological molecule, from the six carbon ring of glucose to the long fatty acid tails found in cell membranes.

The distinction between nonpolar and polar covalent bonds introduced here is not just a chemistry detail; it is the foundation for the next two sections of this chapter. Hydrogen bonds, covered next, can only form because certain covalent bonds, particularly the bond between oxygen and hydrogen, are polar enough to create the partial charges that a hydrogen bond depends on. Water polarity, covered later, is really just this same polar covalent bond principle applied specifically to the water molecule, where it produces the unusual and biologically essential behavior of liquid water.
